text.p: Bonds eased as the leftwing win in France put markets under pressure. Traders were anxiously awaiting news of the new government's budgetary policies.

With the row between the Bundesbank and Bonn over the revaluation of gold reserves still rumbling, the French election result was seen casting fresh doubts on whether monetary union would be launched on time, traders said.

"The two fundamental axis of the future single currency (France and Germany) are in difficulty and are going to provoke instability in southern (European) markets," said Mario Pires of Credit Lyonnais.

"The spreads (10 years vs Bund) have been at record lows on the assumption that the single currency will start on time and the two (Iberian) countries will enter in the first wave," he added. "Amidst these doubts about the euro, we are going to see the whole curve moving upwards," he added.
"I am very sceptical about the fiscal rigour of a new French government, and with Bonn and the Bundesbank at war, the market is going to suffer," said one broker who asked not to be named.
Traders said that the weaker escudo would stop the curve steepening with it unlikely that the Bank of Portugal would cut rates on Tuesday for the start of a new reserve period.
The political war of words in Portugal over opposition plans for a sharp increase in local authority funding had so far had little impact on markets, traders said.
The Socialist government has threatened early elections if the major opposition party, the Social Democrats, does not modify proposals its says would break its budget.
